name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Matching subatomic particles with their characteristics

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Particle) List II (Characteristic / Nature)
A. Electron I. Helium nucleus carrying two units of positive charge and four units of atomic mass
B. Proton II. Electrically neutral particle discovered by bombarding a thin sheet of beryllium with \(\alpha\)-particles
C. Neutron III. Smallest and lightest positive ion obtained from hydrogen gas
D. \(\alpha\)-Particle IV. Constituent particle of cathode rays carrying a negative charge

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Subatomic Particles
Atoms are composed of fundamental subatomic particles whose physical properties, mass, and charge were discovered through specific classical experiments.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Particle
Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles called electrons, whose mass and charge were measured through deflection experiments.
The canal rays or anode rays produced from hydrogen gas yield the lightest and smallest positively charged ion, which is identified as the proton.
James Chadwick discovered electrically neutral particles with a mass slightly greater than that of a proton by bombarding a thin beryllium sheet with \(\alpha\)-particles, naming them neutrons.
Rutherford identified \(\alpha\)-particles as helium nuclei, each carrying two units of positive charge and four units of mass (\(\text{He}^{2+}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Electron corresponds to the constituent particle of cathode rays carrying a negative charge; Proton corresponds to the smallest and lightest positive ion obtained from hydrogen gas; Neutron corresponds to the electrically neutral particle discovered by bombarding beryllium with \(\alpha\)-particles; and \(\alpha\)-Particle corresponds to the helium nucleus carrying two units of positive charge and four units of atomic mass.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Matching quantum numbers with their physical significance

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Quantum Number) List II (Physical Significance)
A. Principal quantum number (\(n\)) I. Gives information about spatial orientation of the orbital with respect to coordinate axes
B. Azimuthal quantum number (\(l\)) II. Defines the three-dimensional shape of the orbital
C. Magnetic orbital quantum number (\(m_l\)) III. Identifies the shell, determines orbital size and to a large extent the orbital energy
D. Electron spin quantum number (\(m_s\)) IV. Refers to the orientation of the intrinsic spin of the electron

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Quantum Numbers
Four quantum numbers are required to completely characterize an electron in an atom. Three arise directly from the solution of Schrödinger's wave equation, while the fourth accounts for the intrinsic angular momentum of the electron.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Quantum Number
The principal quantum number (\(n\)) defines the shell, dictates the orbital size, and largely determines the energy of the orbital.
The azimuthal quantum number (\(l\)), also termed orbital angular momentum or subsidiary quantum number, defines the subshell and the three-dimensional shape of the orbital.
The magnetic orbital quantum number (\(m_l\)) specifies the spatial orientation of the orbital in space relative to a standard coordinate system.
The electron spin quantum number (\(m_s\)) describes the orientation of the intrinsic spin angular momentum of the electron, having values of \(+\frac{1}{2}\) or \(-\frac{1}{2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Principal quantum number with shell identification and orbital size; Azimuthal quantum number with three-dimensional orbital shape; Magnetic orbital quantum number with spatial orientation; and Electron spin quantum number with intrinsic electron spin orientation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Matching spectral series of hydrogen with transitions

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Hydrogen Spectral Series) List II (Lower Energy Level and Spectral Region)
A. Lyman series I. \(n_1 = 2\), \(n_2 = 3, 4, \dots\) (Visible region)
B. Balmer series II. \(n_1 = 1\), \(n_2 = 2, 3, \dots\) (Ultraviolet region)
C. Paschen series III. \(n_1 = 5\), \(n_2 = 6, 7, \dots\) (Infrared region)
D. Pfund series IV. \(n_1 = 3\), \(n_2 = 4, 5, \dots\) (Infrared region)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Rydberg Formula and Spectral Transitions
The wavenumber of radiation emitted during electronic transitions in atomic hydrogen is given by Rydberg's formula: \[\bar{\nu} = 109,677 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)\text{ cm}^{-1}\] where \(n_1\) defines the lower stationary state and \(n_2 > n_1\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Series
Transitions ending at the ground state \(n_1 = 1\) correspond to the Lyman series and lie in the ultraviolet region.
Transitions ending at \(n_1 = 2\) belong to the Balmer series and are the only spectral lines in hydrogen that appear in the visible region.
Transitions ending at \(n_1 = 3\) define the Paschen series, which falls in the infrared region.
Transitions ending at \(n_1 = 5\) define the Pfund series, which also lies in the infrared region.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Lyman series with \(n_1 = 1\) in the ultraviolet region; Balmer series with \(n_1 = 2\) in the visible region; Paschen series with \(n_1 = 3\) in the infrared region; and Pfund series with \(n_1 = 5\) in the infrared region.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Matching scientists with their atomic theories

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Scientist) List II (Contribution / Concept)
A. Max Planck I. Dual behaviour of matter proposing wave properties for material particles
B. Albert Einstein II. Quantization of electromagnetic radiation into discrete packets called quanta
C. Louis de Broglie III. Principle ruling out the simultaneous exact determination of position and momentum
D. Werner Heisenberg IV. Theoretical explanation of photoelectric effect using particle-like light photons

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Historical Scientific Developments
The early twentieth century witnessed the transition from classical physics to quantum theory through key insights into radiation and matter.

Step 2: Analysis of Individual Contributions
Max Planck proposed in 1900 that radiant energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets called quanta, establishing \(E = h\nu\).
Albert Einstein in 1905 extended Planck's theory to explain the photoelectric effect, showing that light consists of discrete energy particles called photons.
Louis de Broglie in 1924 proposed that just as radiation has particle properties, matter also exhibits wave-particle duality (\(\lambda = h/p\)).
Werner Heisenberg in 1927 stated the uncertainty principle, demonstrating that position and momentum of a microscopic particle cannot be simultaneously determined with arbitrary precision.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Max Planck with quantization of radiant energy into discrete quanta; Albert Einstein with explanation of photoelectric effect using photons; Louis de Broglie with dual behaviour of matter; and Werner Heisenberg with uncertainty principle regarding position and momentum.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Matching electronic filling rules with statements

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Rule / Principle) List II (Statement / Consequence)
A. Aufbau principle I. No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers
B. Pauli exclusion principle II. In the ground state of atoms, orbitals are filled in order of their increasing energies
C. Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity III. Pairing of electrons in degenerate orbitals does not occur until each orbital is singly occupied
D. Heisenberg uncertainty principle IV. Rules out the existence of fixed circular orbits or definite trajectories for electrons

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Concepts of Orbital Filling
The distribution of electrons in atomic orbitals is regulated by three main principles, while quantum mechanics sets the boundary limits on electron localization.

Step 2: Detailed Principles Analysis
Aufbau principle states that electrons first occupy the lowest energy orbital available and progressively fill orbitals in order of increasing energy.
Pauli exclusion principle dictates that no two electrons in an atom can possess the identical set of four quantum numbers, which limits each orbital to a maximum of two electrons with opposed spins.
Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that pairing of electrons within a degenerate subshell (\(p\), \(d\), or \(f\)) begins only after each orbital has received one electron with parallel spin.
Heisenberg uncertainty principle establishes that the simultaneous precise measurement of position and momentum of an electron is impossible, disproving fixed planetary trajectories or Bohr orbits.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Aufbau principle with filling orbitals in order of increasing energy; Pauli exclusion principle with no two electrons having identical four quantum numbers; Hund's rule with pairing occurring only after single occupancy; and Heisenberg uncertainty principle with ruling out definite electron trajectories.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Matching electromagnetic radiation regions with frequencies

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Radiation Type) List II (Characteristic Frequency / Application)
A. Radio frequency region I. Around \(10^{16}\text{ Hz}\), component of sun's radiation
B. Microwave region II. Around \(10^{13}\text{ Hz}\), used for heating
C. Infrared region III. Around \(10^{10}\text{ Hz}\), used for radar
D. Ultraviolet region IV. Around \(10^{6}\text{ Hz}\), used for broadcasting

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electromagnetic Spectrum Overview
Electromagnetic radiation consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields traveling through vacuum at \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}\), spanning diverse frequencies and applications.

Step 2: Frequency Region Identifications
The radio frequency region lies around \(10^{6}\text{ Hz}\) and is utilized for broadcasting.
The microwave region lies around \(10^{10}\text{ Hz}\) and is used for radar systems.
The infrared region lies around \(10^{13}\text{ Hz}\) and is associated with thermal heating.
The ultraviolet region lies around \(10^{16}\text{ Hz}\) and forms an important component of solar radiation reaching the earth's atmosphere.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Radio frequency region with \(10^6\text{ Hz}\) for broadcasting; Microwave region with \(10^{10}\text{ Hz}\) for radar; Infrared region with \(10^{13}\text{ Hz}\) for heating; and Ultraviolet region with \(10^{16}\text{ Hz}\) as a component of sun's radiation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Matching atomic orbitals with nodal features

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Orbital) List II (Shape and Number of Radial / Angular Nodes)
A. \(2s\) orbital I. Spherically symmetric with 1 radial node and 0 angular nodes
B. \(2p\) orbital II. Dumbbell shape with 0 radial nodes and 1 angular node
C. \(3p\) orbital III. Dumbbell shape with 1 radial node and 1 angular node
D. \(3d\) orbital IV. Cloverleaf / complex shape with 0 radial nodes and 2 angular nodes

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formulae for Nodal Surfaces in Orbitals
For any atomic orbital characterized by principal quantum number \(n\) and azimuthal quantum number \(l\):
Number of radial nodes \(= n - l - 1\)
Number of angular nodes \(= l\)
Total number of nodes \(= n - 1\)

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculation for Each Orbital
For \(2s\): \(n = 2, l = 0\). Radial nodes \(= 2 - 0 - 1 = 1\), angular nodes \(= 0\). The shape is spherically symmetric.
For \(2p\): \(n = 2, l = 1\). Radial nodes \(= 2 - 1 - 1 = 0\), angular nodes \(= 1\). The shape is dumbbell-shaped.
For \(3p\): \(n = 3, l = 1\). Radial nodes \(= 3 - 1 - 1 = 1\), angular nodes \(= 1\). The shape is dumbbell-shaped.
For \(3d\): \(n = 3, l = 2\). Radial nodes \(= 3 - 2 - 1 = 0\), angular nodes \(= 2\). The shape consists of four lobes (cloverleaf) or double dumbbell with a doughnut.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: \(2s\) orbital with spherically symmetric shape having 1 radial and 0 angular nodes; \(2p\) orbital with dumbbell shape having 0 radial and 1 angular nodes; \(3p\) orbital with dumbbell shape having 1 radial and 1 angular nodes; and \(3d\) orbital with complex four-lobed shape having 0 radial and 2 angular nodes.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Matching physical equations with fundamental principles

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Mathematical Relation) List II (Associated Law / Postulate)
A. \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}\) I. Conservation of energy in photoelectric emission
B. \(\Delta x \times \Delta p_x \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}\) II. Quantization of orbital angular momentum in stationary states
C. \(m_e v r = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\) III. Principle governing the fundamental limit on simultaneous measurement of conjugate variables
D. \(h\nu = h\nu_0 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_e v^2\) IV. de Broglie relationship for matter wave wavelength

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Foundational Equations of Modern Atomic Physics
Each mathematical relation embodies a fundamental postulate or conservation law established during the development of quantum atomic theory.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Mathematical Relation
The expression \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{p}\) represents the de Broglie equation relating the wavelength of matter waves to particle momentum.
The inequality \(\Delta x \times \Delta p_x \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}\) constitutes the mathematical formulation of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, establishing fundamental limits on simultaneous measurements of position and momentum.
The formula \(m_e v r = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\) represents Niels Bohr's quantum condition postulating that orbital angular momentum of an electron is quantized as an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\).
The equation \(h\nu = h\nu_0 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_e v^2\) is Einstein's photoelectric equation expressing energy conservation, where incident photon energy is partitioned into metal work function (\(h\nu_0\)) and photoelectron kinetic energy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}\) with de Broglie matter wave relationship; \(\Delta x \times \Delta p_x \ge \dfrac{h}{4\pi}\) with Heisenberg uncertainty principle; \(m_e v r = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\) with quantization of orbital angular momentum; and \(h\nu = h\nu_0 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_e v^2\) with photoelectric conservation of energy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Matching transition metals with valence configurations

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Element and Atomic Number) List II (Ground State Valence Shell Configuration)
A. Chromium (\(Z = 24\)) I. \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1\)
B. Copper (\(Z = 29\)) II. \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1\)
C. Iron (\(Z = 26\)) III. \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^1\,4s^2\)
D. Scandium (\(Z = 21\)) IV. \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electronic Configuration Principles and Exceptional Stabilities
Electrons fill orbitals following the \((n+l)\) rule. However, half-filled (\(d^5\)) and fully filled (\(d^{10}\)) subshells possess extra stability due to symmetrical distribution of electron density and maximum exchange energy.

Step 2: Analysis of Each Element
For Chromium (\(Z = 24\)), instead of the expected \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^4\,4s^2\), an electron shifts from \(4s\) to \(3d\) to acquire a half-filled \(d^5\) subshell, resulting in \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1\).
For Copper (\(Z = 29\)), instead of \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^9\,4s^2\), an electron shifts from \(4s\) to \(3d\) to acquire a completely filled \(d^{10}\) subshell, resulting in \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1\).
For Iron (\(Z = 26\)), the configuration follows the regular Aufbau sequence: \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2\).
For Scandium (\(Z = 21\)), \(4s\) is filled before \(3d\), yielding \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^1\,4s^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Chromium with \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1\); Copper with \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1\); Iron with \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2\); and Scandium with \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^1\,4s^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STRUCTURE_OF_ATOM_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Matching atomic parameters with mathematical formulas

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Atomic Parameter) List II (Mathematical Expression)
A. Radius of \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit for hydrogen-like species (\(r_n\)) I. \(-2.18 \times 10^{-18} \left(\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\right)\text{ J}\)
B. Energy of \(n^{\text{th}}\) stationary state for hydrogen-like species (\(E_n\)) II. \(\dfrac{52.9\,(n^2)}{Z}\text{ pm}\)
C. Maximum number of electrons accommodated in shell with principal quantum number \(n\) III. \(2n^2\)
D. Total number of allowed orbitals in shell with principal quantum number \(n\) IV. \(n^2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Bohr's Model and Quantum Shell Relationships
Bohr derived exact quantitative relations for one-electron (hydrogen-like) systems depending on nuclear charge \(Z\) and principal quantum level \(n\), while quantum mechanics defines orbital and electron capacities per principal shell.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Expression
The radius of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) stationary orbit for a hydrogen-like system is given by \(r_n = \dfrac{52.9\,(n^2)}{Z}\text{ pm}\).
The energy associated with the \(n^{\text{th}}\) stationary level is given by \(E_n = -2.18 \times 10^{-18} \left(\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\right)\text{ J}\).
According to Pauli exclusion principle, an orbital can hold at most two electrons, so the maximum electron capacity of shell \(n\) is \(2n^2\).
The total number of allowed orbitals in a shell with principal quantum number \(n\) is given by the summation \(\sum_{l=0}^{n-1} (2l+1) = n^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: Radius of \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit with \(\dfrac{52.9\,(n^2)}{Z}\text{ pm}\); Energy of \(n^{\text{th}}\) stationary state with \(-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\right)\text{ J}\); Maximum electron capacity with \(2n^2\); and Total number of allowed orbitals with \(n^2\).
